unit.title: Mixing materials
unit.blurb: Solids, liquids and gases, mixtures, sieving, dissolving, filtering and materials from rocks.

O1.t: Sort materials into solids, liquids and gases, and describe how each behaves.

O2.t: Know what a mixture is, and separate a mixture by picking out or sieving.

O3.t: Know that some solids dissolve in water and some do not, and that warmth and stirring help.

O4.t: Use a filter to separate an insoluble solid from water, and know filtered water is not safe to drink.

O5.t: Know that useful materials come from rocks, and that magnets and evaporation can separate them.

q.prompt: Which one keeps its own shape?

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Everything around us is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
This is lesson 2.1: solids, liquids and gases.
A solid keeps its own shape.
A brick is a solid. A stone is a solid.
You can hold a solid in your hand.
Your teddy and an apple are solids too!
A liquid can flow and pour.
Water, milk and juice are liquids.
A liquid takes the shape of its container.
Pour juice into a cup. It becomes cup-shaped!
Pause and think.
Which one is a liquid?
A gas spreads out everywhere.
Air is a gas. We cannot see it, but we can feel it on a windy day.
Blow up a balloon. It fills with air!
Steam from a hot kettle is a gas too.
Look at your breakfast table!
The toast is a solid. It keeps its shape.
The milk is a liquid. It pours.
The steam from a hot drink is a gas. It floats away!
Did you know?
Water can be all three!
Ice is solid water. Water is a liquid. And steam is water as a gas.
Riddle time!
What gets wetter and wetter the more it dries?
A towel!
Your turn.
Which one keeps its own shape?
Let's do a kitchen sort!
Look around your kitchen, with an adult.
Find a solid, like a spoon. Find a liquid, like milk.
Can you find something with a gas inside? A fizzy drink has gas bubbles!
Let's remember.
A solid keeps its own shape.
A liquid flows, and takes the shape of its container.
A gas spreads out everywhere.
And air is a gas. Super sorting!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
What happens when we mix things? Can we get them back out?
This is lesson 2.2: separating mixtures.
Get a bowl.
Put in some rice and some peas.
Stir them up.
Now we have a mixture! A mixture is two or more things mixed together.
Can we separate the mixture?
Separate means to take apart.
Yes! We can pick out the peas with our fingers.
Now the peas and the rice are separate again.
Pause and think.
What is a mixture?
Picking out takes a long time.
Here is a faster way: a sieve!
A sieve has small holes. Small things fall through. Big things stay in.
Shake sand and pebbles in a sieve. The sand falls through. The pebbles stay!
We use sieves at home.
A colander drains water from pasta.
A flour sieve takes lumps out of flour.
And at the beach, you can sieve sand to find shells!
Did you know?
Long ago, people shook mud from rivers in big pans.
They were looking for tiny pieces of gold!
Riddle time!
What has lots of holes, but can still hold things?
A sieve!
Your turn.
What is the best way to separate sand and pebbles?
Let's try a sieve challenge!
Mix some rice and some dried beans in a bowl.
Pour the mixture into a sieve, and shake it gently over another bowl.
What falls through? What stays in the sieve?
Let's remember.
A mixture is two or more things mixed together.
Separate means to take apart.
We can pick things out with our fingers.
Or use a sieve. Big bits stay in. Small bits fall through. Great separating!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Where does sugar go when you put it in water? Let's find out!
This is lesson 2.3: dissolving.
Get a glass of warm water.
Add a spoon of sugar.
Stir, stir, stir.
Where did the sugar go? We cannot see it any more!
Think about sweet tea. You cannot see the sugar, but the tea tastes sweet.
So the sugar is still there!
The sugar broke into tiny, tiny bits, too small to see.
We say the sugar dissolved.
Pause and think.
What happens to sugar when you stir it into water?
Some things dissolve in water.
Sugar and salt dissolve.
Some things do not dissolve.
Sand and pebbles just sink to the bottom.
Can we make sugar dissolve faster?
Yes! Use warm water.
And stir it.
Warm water and stirring make things dissolve faster.
Did you know?
The sea tastes salty.
That is because lots of salt is dissolved in the water!
Joke time!
Why did the sugar go swimming?
Because it wanted to dissolve all its problems!
Your turn.
Which one will dissolve in water?
Let's do a dissolving test.
Put water in three cups.
Add sugar to one, salt to one, and sand to one.
Stir each cup. Which ones disappear? Which one sinks?
Let's remember.
When something dissolves, it breaks into tiny bits in water.
Sugar and salt dissolve.
Sand and pebbles do not dissolve.
And warm water and stirring make dissolving faster. Sweet work!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
How can we clean muddy water? Let's find out!
This is lesson 2.4: filtering.
Here is some muddy water.
Can we use a sieve? No!
The mud is too small. It goes through the holes.
We need a filter.
A filter has very, very tiny holes.
Put a paper towel in a funnel, over a jar.
Pour the muddy water in.
Drip, drip. Cleaner water comes out! The mud stays in the paper.
Pause and think.
What does a filter take out of muddy water?
Filters are everywhere!
A tea bag is a filter. The tea leaves stay inside.
A coffee filter keeps the coffee grounds out.
And a fish tank has a filter to keep the water clean.
Here is an important rule.
Filtered muddy water looks cleaner, but it is not safe to drink.
Tiny germs can still get through.
Never drink water from your experiments.
Did you know?
Some huge whales have filters in their mouths.
They gulp seawater and keep the tiny food inside!
Riddle time!
What is full of holes, but can still hold water?
A sponge!
Your turn.
Which one is a filter?
Let's make a filter.
Mix some soil and water in a cup.
Put a paper towel in a funnel, over a jar, and pour the muddy water in.
Look at the water in the jar. Now look at the paper. Where is the mud?
Let's remember.
A filter has very, very tiny holes.
It can take mud and bits out of water.
Tea bags and coffee filters are filters.
And never drink water from experiments. Fantastic filtering!

q.prompt: How do we get salt from seawater?

options.t: Let the Sun dry up the water

twin.prompt: Seawater dries up in the sun. What is left?

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Many useful things come from rocks! How do we get them out?
This is lesson 2.5: separating materials from rocks.
People dig rocks out of the ground.
Some rocks have metals inside them, like iron.
We use the metal to make cars, spoons and bridges!
But first we must separate the metal from the rock.
Some rock dust has tiny bits of iron in it.
Iron sticks to a magnet.
Move a magnet over the dust.
Whoosh! The iron bits jump onto the magnet. The sand stays behind!
Pause and think.
What can pull iron bits out of sand?
We get salt from the sea.
People put seawater in big, flat pools.
The hot Sun warms the water, and the water goes into the air.
White salt is left behind. That is the salt on your food!
So we know lots of ways to separate things.
We can pick out with our fingers.
We can use a sieve or a filter.
And a magnet pulls out iron!
Did you know?
Sparkly diamonds are found inside rocks, deep under the ground!
Joke time!
What kind of music do rocks like best?
Rock music, of course!
Your turn.
How do we get salt from seawater?
Let's make salt crystals!
Dissolve some salt in warm water, with an adult.
Pour a little of the salty water onto a plate, and leave it in a sunny place.
Look after a few days. Sparkly salt is left on the plate!
Let's remember.
Some rocks have useful metals inside.
A magnet can pull iron bits out of sand.
We get salt by letting seawater dry up.
And there are many ways to separate mixtures. Rock-star work!
